function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 50 -- Permission to Begin
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: Cycle 1,892. The original six-month preparation timeline from Cycle 1,359 has been extended four times. The colony voted to defer: twelve months, then eighteen, then another year. It is now five years and four months since Sana and Tariq first stood in Laila's medbay and asked a question. The question has not been answered with a date. But it has been answered with work. -- MAI*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|The third greenhouse rack had been online for eleven months. The colony ate tomatoes with casualness now -- the Martian meaning, the one that said the experience was no longer remarkable. Margin. Laila needed margin.
    10|
    11|She stood in the medbay, expanded into Hab 2's former storage bay. Wider. Second surgical area. An incubator built by Arun's team and tested seven times. Redundant power. Tested.
    12|
    13|On her desk sat a binder. Two hundred fourteen pages, two-sided, Arial 11pt: *Martian Reproductive Preparedness: Medical Protocol Version 3.1.* The version number tracked five years of iteration. V1.0 was a gap analysis. V2.0 incorporated the expansion. V3.0 was reviewed by fourteen specialists on Earth during a two-week data burst window. V3.1 was the final draft.
    14|
    15|She had been staring at it for forty minutes. The words had become shapes now -- *fetal radiation dose, low-gravity delivery positioning, emergency cesarean protocol* -- and none of them felt like enough. The document was comprehensive. It had been reviewed by seventeen people. It was the best medical preparedness document ever written for a planet where no human had ever been born.
    16|
    17|No document could bridge the gap between what was known and what could only be discovered by doing.
    18|
    19|"A knock at the medbay door. Sana walked in. Tariq behind her. They looked older -- of course they did. Five years had passed. Sana's hair had greyed at the temples, cut short now, practical. Tariq had put on weight -- the healthy kind, from eating enough calories and not rationing.
    20|
    21|"We heard there's a meeting," Sana said.
    22|
    23|"There's a meeting."
    24|
    25|"You're presenting today."
    26|
    27|"I'm presenting."
    28|
    29|Tariq shifted his weight. "And then what." Laila met his eyes. She had known this couple since they arrived on Mars. She had known them before they were a couple -- during the descent, when they were two frightened people in two separate crash couches, three ships apart, not speaking, not knowing if they would survive their first Martian night. She had known them through the early settlement years, when they found each other in the common area one evening and started sitting at the same table. She had known them through Carlos's death, through the blackout, through the unauthorized experiment, through the construction of Jonah's hall. She had known them through the first question, the one in this medbay, five years and four months ago.
    30|
    31|She had been watching them wait for half a decade.
    32|
    33|"And then," Laila said, "the colony votes. That's the plan."
    34|
    35|"If the plan works."
    36|
    37|"If the plan works. But I'm going to need you two to understand something before we go in there. The document I wrote -- it's not a permission slip. It's not a guarantee. It's a list of everything we know about what could go wrong and everything we've built to handle it. It is thorough. It is honest. And it is still not enough to make the risk zero. I need you to understand this because if the vote goes through, it goes through with conditions. Conditions that you will have to live with every day of a pregnancy. It will not be a private medical relationship. It will be the entire colony invested in your outcome. Every caloric surplus, every engineering redundancy, every hour of labor -- the colony will be participating in your pregnancy whether they like it or not. And some of them won't like it."
    38|
    39|Sana looked at Tariq. Tariq looked at the floor, then at Laila.
    40|
    41|"We know," he said. "We've known that for five years."
    42|
    43|"Good. Then let's go. The hall."
    44|
    45|---
    46|
    47|*The buried connector hall held more people now than it had during the first gathering about children. The colony was larger -- thirty-nine souls, up from thirty-three. Six new arrivals from the last crew, people who had come to Mars not in the first desperate wave but in the deliberate second wave, the wave that came because the first wave had not died. They sat in the hall with the gravity of people who understood that they were witnesses to a decision they had not been present for when it was first asked.*
    48|
    49|The hall held thirty-nine people. The anchor bolts remained, Jonah's permanent work, but the room had grown -- insulation on the walls, a smoother floor, better lighting. It had become the place where the colony marked transitions.
    50|
    51|Elena sat at the front. Tired, but the steady kind that comes from work that matters. Her hair was shorter now, streaked with grey. She held a tablet and a pen -- habit and future, the bridge between them.
    52|
    53|The colony assembled. Originals: Elena, Arun, Imani, Gabriel, Laila, Nadia, Tomas, Sana, Tariq. The newer arrivals -- six people who had come to Mars because the first wave had not died. People sitting in a buried room with a question that had been asked five years ago and answered with five years of work.
    54|
    55|*Elena stood.*
    56|
    57|*"Five years ago, Dr. Okonkwo presented the medical case for why having children on Mars was risky. At that time, she was right. I called for six months of preparation. The colony extended that timeline. Six months became a year, then two, then five. Not because we were running away from the decision. Because we understood that preparation on Mars means building something, not just studying something."*
    58|
    59|*She gestured to Laila.*
    60|
    61|*"Dr. Okonkwo will present the current medical picture. Then we will vote. Not on whether to have children today. On whether to allow carefully planned pregnancies under strict medical support, with colony-wide infrastructure. This is not a green light for recklessness. It is a framework for responsibility. A plan that, if approved, means that Sana and Tariq -- and anyone else who wants to follow -- can begin the process of becoming parents on Mars. With oversight. With resources. With the entire colony behind them."*
    62|
    63|*She sat down.*
    64|
    65|*Laila stood.*
    66|
    67|*The document in her binder was comprehensive. She did not need to read it aloud. She needed to tell the colony what it meant.*
    68|
    69|---
    70|
    71|## Scene 2
    72|
    73|"This is not a risk assessment," Laila said. "This is a capability assessment. That's the difference between five years ago and today."
    74|
    75|She stood at the center of the hall, a small table set up beside her with three objects: the binder, a model incubator -- the real one, not the prototype, sitting in the corner of the medbay right now -- and a small sealed vial containing synthetic blood substitute, one of the colony's newest technical achievements.
    76|
    77|"Five years ago, I listed four categories of unknown. Low-gravity fetal development. Radiation exposure. Surgical capacity. And the child's long-term future. I'm going to address each one. Not to tell you that they're solved. To tell you that they're understood."
    78|
    79|She tapped the binder.
    80|
    81|"First: low-gravity fetal development. We still do not have human data. We never will until someone does it. What we do have is more complete animal modeling than existed five years ago. The colony's biology lab, under Mei's direction, has been running a controlled study on gestating rodents for the past eighteen months. Not mice. Rats -- larger, closer to human developmental timelines. Three generations now, all conceived and born at Mars gravity. The results: no gross developmental anomalies. Bone mineralization is twelve to eighteen percent lower than Earth controls -- consistent with what we see in adult bone loss on Mars, but stable, meaning the animals' bodies adapted to Mars gravity as their baseline. The vestibular system develops normally -- the inner ear, which is gravity-sensitive, functions within normal parameters. Cardiovascular structure is slightly different -- lower blood pressure, larger heart chambers relative to body size -- but the animals are healthy. They move, they eat, they breed, they live. They are Martian rats. They are not broken rats. They are rats adapted to a new environment."
    82|
    83|She paused. Let the distinction sink in.
    84|
    85|"This does not translate directly to humans. Rats are not humans. But it is the best evidence we have that thirty-eight percent gravity is sufficient for mammalian fetal development. It does not guarantee a healthy human pregnancy. It removes one layer of terror from the unknown."
    86|
    87|Arun raised his hand. "Twelve to eighteen percent lower bone mineralization. What does that mean for a child. If they grow up with that deficit, can they ever reach Earth-normal bone density."
    88|
    89|"Good question. On Earth, peak bone mass is achieved in late adolescence. A Martian child would reach their peak bone mass at Martian levels -- lower than Earth baseline. If that child were exposed to Earth gravity as an adult, it would be a significant physiological stress. We don't know if their bones could adapt. The rat study ran three generations -- all born on Mars, all healthy. We have not exposed Martian-born rats to Earth gravity. That's a study we cannot design here."
    90|
    91|Arun nodded slowly. "So the answer is: the child will be Martian. And if they visit Earth, it would be a medical challenge."
    92|
    93|"Yes. But it would be their challenge, not ours. We are not making a decision for a future adult. We are making a decision for a child who will be born here, who will grow up here, who will be Martian in a way that none of us ever will be. That is not a reason to say no. It is a reason to be honest about what yes means."
    94|
    95|Nadia raised her hand. The same Nadia who had opposed the archive allocation five years ago, who had argued about water rationing during the first drought, who had since become the colony's most reliable logistical mind. She had learned to balance short-term costs against long-term value. Laila could see that learning in the way she framed her question.
    96|
    97|"Caloric impact. You presented fourteen percent surplus five years ago. Where are we now."
    98|
    99|Laila nodded to Arun, who stood.
   100|
   101|"Twenty-eight percent surplus on average, with the third greenhouse rack online and the second water extraction point operational at Site Beta. We buffer at twenty-two percent minimum, which accounts for crop failure, solar events, and equipment downtime. A pregnancy in the third trimester requires approximately three hundred additional calories per day for the mother. Postpartum lactation requires five hundred. The surplus absorbs both with room to spare. If we have two pregnancies overlapping, we'd drop to sixteen percent surplus -- still above our safety threshold. We can handle two concurrent pregnancies. A third would require rationing or expansion of the greenhouse."
   102|
   103|"Two at once is more than we're planning," Laila added. "The vote today is for *carefully planned* pregnancies. Planned means one at a time, with colony-wide awareness and resource allocation. We're not trying to repopulate Mars. We're trying to see if Mars can host a single human birth."
   104|
   105|Imani's hand went up before Laila called on her. Imani had aged in the way that pilots age -- not with grey in their hair, but with a stillness in their posture, a way of sitting that suggested they were always ready for the seatbelt light to come on. She had been right about expansion and children being the same argument. She had been right about using the children question to justify Site Beta. She had been right about almost everything, and she had never been satisfied with being right.
   106|
   107|"Imani."
   108|
   109|Imani's eyes widened slightly.
   110|
   111|"You have steady hands," Laila continued. "Your EVA experience means you can work under pressure. You've observed six simulations. You are not a surgeon. You are not a doctor. But if I am incapacitated during a delivery, you can maintain a cesarean until I recover or until the baby is delivered. It's not ideal. But it means I am not alone anymore. The second is Nadia, who has a background in veterinary medicine before she came to Mars. Nadia has reviewed the procedure. Nadia has demonstrated proficiency on the simulation mannequin. Two people, plus me. Three people who can sustain a delivery if the primary operator -- me -- is unavailable."
   112|
   113|"Simulations." Nadia added. "We have run twelve full procedural simulations -- emergency cesarean, neonatal resuscitation, maternal hemorrhage control. Each simulation has been timed, recorded, and reviewed. The twelfth simulation had a completion time of forty-seven minutes from incision to delivery of the infant, with both mother and neonate stable. That includes the time required to don surgical prep -- which takes three minutes longer on Mars because the gravity affects the way fluids pool and the way the drapes settle. Forty-seven minutes is comparable to -- and in some cases faster than -- Earth-based emergency cesarean benchmarks."
   114|
   115|"That's encouraging," Imani said.
   116|
   117|"It's promising," Laila corrected. "Encouraging is what you feel after a good simulation. Promising is what the data says. They are different things. But the data is the best we have."
   118|
   119|She set the binder down. She stood very still, looking out across the faces of the colony -- people who had waited five years, people who had prepared for this, people who would be affected by the outcome of what happened in this room.
   120|
   121|"What we do not know: I will not pretend these five years have eliminated uncertainty. They have not. We still do not know what Mars gravity will do to a human child. We still do not know what radiation exposure -- even at current reduced rates -- will do to germline stability. We still do not know what a baby will look like, sound like, feel like, when it is born under this planet. The simulations are not the thing. The binder is not the thing. The incubator and the blood substitute and the trained backup are not the thing. The thing is a pregnancy. The thing is a child. The thing is a person who has never existed and who may or may not survive the process of existing."
   122|
   123|She felt the room lean in. Not dramatically. Not theatrically. The way a colony leans in when it understands that the person at the front of the room is about to say something that cannot be un-said.
   124|
   125|"This is not safe."
   126|
   127|The words came out quietly, but they carried. They always carried, in the hall.
   128|
   129|"Medicine is not saying this is safe. Medicine cannot say this is safe because this is not safe. It is the most risky thing any human being on this planet has ever attempted. And it needs to happen anyway."
   130|
   131|---
   132|
   133|## Scene 3
   134|
   135|Laila had rehearsed the next part. She had written it, read it, changed it, read it again, and then discarded the writing and decided she would say it from her own mouth, not from the binder, because the binder was the science and what she was about to say was not science.
   136|
   137|She set the binder on the table. She let her hands rest on its cover. Paper, under fingers. Real, tactile, present.
   138|
   139|"I want to be very clear about what I am telling you. I want you to hear me the first time because I will not say it differently the second time."
   140|
   141|She looked at every face in the room. Not sequentially. All at once, the way she had learned to do when she was about to say something the colony needed to hold together.
   142|
   143|"Five years ago, I told Sana and Tariq that I would never be ready. That was honest then. It is still honest now. What has changed is not my readiness. What has changed is the colony's *capacity to absorb risk.*"
   144|
   145|She let the phrase land.
   146|
   147|"Capacity to absorb risk. That is what engineering calls it when you build a system with enough redundancy that a single failure does not cascade into catastrophe. We have built that capacity. We have the incubator with its redundant power. We have the blood substitute with four-liter reserve. We have three people who can perform an emergency cesarean -- not because any of us went to medical school, but because we spent twelve hundred hours practicing on a mannequin until our hands knew what to do. We have the caloric surplus. We have the water. We have the power redundancy. We have the Site Beta ice extraction that makes water a thing we do not worry about. We have the greenhouse that makes food a thing we can plan around."
   148|
   149|She picked up the binder again, but she did not open it. She held it against her chest, the way a person holds something they care about, and she spoke.
   150|
   151|"We have prepared as much as preparation can prepare you for something that has never happened. And I want you to understand the plain truth of what that means."
   152|
   153|She took a breath. In the silence of the hall, the ventilation fans sounded like the ventilation fans had sounded in every meeting since the colony was founded: steady, constant, the sound of a machine keeping people alive while they argued and cried and loved each other.
   154|
   155|"The plain truth is this: medicine is not saying it is safe. Medicine is saying they -- meaning I, meaning the fourteen specialists on Earth, meaning the three of us in the medbay who have spent five years studying this problem -- medicine is saying that we finally understand the risks well enough to choose responsibly. I am not asking you to vote for a safe pregnancy. I am asking you to vote for a *comprehended* one. A pregnancy where every risk has been catalogued, every failure mode has been rehearsed, every known variable has been modeled. Where the unknowns have not been eliminated but have been circled and labeled and acknowledged. Where the people who will carry the risk -- Sana, Tariq, the child that does not yet exist -- are asking to take it with full knowledge of what they are asking."
   156|
   157|She set the binder down again. Her hands were steady. She did not feel steady. She felt like she was standing on the edge of something and speaking to everyone who was standing behind her, and she was saying: *I see the edge. I know what it looks like. I know what falling means. I am telling you not that it won't happen, but that we have tied ropes around ourselves and checked the knots seven times and the person who is going to step off the edge has asked to step and wants all of us watching in case she needs to be pulled back.*
   158|
   159|"I am a doctor. I took the Hippocratic Oath before I came to Mars. It says: *First, do no harm. And the oath does not say: First, do no harm, unless the harm is necessary.* But sometimes -- sometimes medicine has to look like something other than harm prevention. Sometimes medicine has to look like informed permission. *I understand the danger. I accept the danger. Will you help me carry it.*"
   160|
   161|She sat down. The binder sat on the table. The incantation sat on the table too, though no one could see it except her.
   162|
   163|She looked up and met Sana's eyes across the room.
   164|
   165|Sana was not crying. She had practiced. But she was crying now -- quiet tears that came from a well that had been full for five years. She wiped them with the back of her hand and set it back in Tariq's grasp.
   166|
   167|Tariq was staring at the anchor bolts on the ceiling, doing the thing Jonah had done when he installed them: looking at structure and seeing the future.
   168|
   169|Imani's hand went up.
   170|
   171|Laila nodded.
   172|
   173|"I want to say something," Imani said. "Not as an advocate. Not as a pilot. As someone who has been part of every expansion argument and every safety argument and who has been right about both and is not satisfied being right about either." She stood and walked to the center of the hall. "I was wrong five years ago when I said *now is better than later.* I thought I was right. I thought I was right because later meant another crisis and another delay and another year of people waiting for permission to hope. But I was wrong. Because *later* became five years. And in those five years, the incubator got built. The blood substitute got formulated. The greenhouse got expanded. The simulations got run twelve times. The medbay got a second surgical suite. The colony got six new members who came because they believed we were building something real, not something temporary."
   174|
   175|She turned and looked at the hall. At the walls that Jonah had built. At the anchor bolts that held the ceiling. At the colony that had waited five years.
   176|
   177|"Later was not a delay. Later was a build. And what we built in those five years is the margin of safety that might save a child's life. That matters. I want to acknowledge that Laila was right to push for preparation. I was impatient. Impatience is not a strategy. It is a feeling. And feelings do not hold babies up."
   178|
   179|Imani sat down. The room was quiet. Then Gabriel's hand went up -- Gabriel, who had been recording everything since the first day, whose archive had become the colony's memory, who had written *The Question. The Question Still Here. Future Tense.* and who now, standing in the hall that held the Archive of the Living, asked a question that was not about data or protocol or surgical capacity but about meaning.
   180|
   181|"Dr. Okonkwo," Gabriel said. "When you say *comprehended risk* -- when you say that medicine is no longer saying *don't* but is saying *choose* -- are you also saying that the child's future is now the colony's responsibility, collectively. Not just Sana and Tariq. Not just the medbay. All of us."
   182|

## Scene 1

The result appeared on Laila's tablet during breakfast. Not at her desk in the medbay, not in a controlled clinical environment, but at the mess hall table where she was half-listening to Mei discuss nitrogen cycling in the third greenhouse rack while pretending to care about nitrogen cycling instead of checking her tablet every forty seconds because Sana was supposed to take the test at 0600 and it was now 0617 and the test needed ten minutes.

She excused herself without standing. She looked at the screen.

POSITIVE. 847 mIU/mL. Four to five weeks estimated.

She stared at the number. 847. A number on a screen, derived from a chemical reaction in a plastic stick, representing a cell cluster the size of a poppy seed, dividing in thirty-eight percent gravity on a planet where no human cell had ever divided before outside a Petri dish.

"I need to go."

"Did it --?"

"I need to go."

She had discussed radiation protocols and emergency procedures and caloric adjustments and the psychological monitoring schedule. She had discussed the possibility of loss -- not in vague terms, but in specific, harrowing detail, because she refused to lie about risk. But she had not sufficiently prepared them for the weight of the colony's collective hope, which was a pressure no medical protocol could measure and no simulation could model.

"I'm going to adjust the plan," Laila said. "Not the medical plan. The social plan. I'm going to designate two times per week when you are off-limits. No colony visits. No check-ins. No casual conversations about how you're feeling in the corridor. Those times are yours. Yours and Tariq's. You spend them however you want. You don't owe the colony a status report. You don't owe me a status report unless something is medically relevant."

Sana's shoulders dropped. Just a fraction. "Thank you."

"I'm also going to establish a communication protocol. Mission AI will broadcast a weekly update -- general, non-invasive. No medical details, no hormone numbers, no ultrasound results unless you authorize me to share them. The update will say one of three things: all is well, there are minor concerns being addressed, or there is a significant development requiring colony attention. That's it. No daily check-in requests. No knock-on-shoulder conversations. If someone wants to send a message, they route it through the AI and the AI filters it for content and frequency. You get no more than five messages per day from non-essential senders."

Tariq looked at her with genuine gratitude. "You can do that."

"I can and I will. The colonists will push back. They'll say they have a right to know. And I'll say that Sana's mental health is a medical variable and stress is a risk factor and if they want this pregnancy to succeed, they need to let the pregnant person breathe."

Sana smiled. It was small, tired, and real. "Can you say that to Elena."

"I just did. She'll support it. She already told me not to let people crowd the medbay. She understands boundaries. Some people don't. We'll educate them."

After they left, Laila updated the colony-wide prenatal care protocol. Not the medical sections -- those were exhaustive, reviewed, and stable. The social sections. The ones that governed how thirty-nine people interacted with two people who were carrying a risk that belonged to everyone. She wrote:

*PROTOCOL UPDATE -- CYCLE 1,918. Designated private hours: Tuesday and Thursday, 1800 to 2200. During these windows, Sana Qureshi and Tariq al-Hassan are not available for colony interaction unless medical emergency. Weekly colony update via Mission AI, Fridays at 1900. Non-essential communication limited to five messages per day per recipient, filtered by AI for supportive content only. No physical contact with the pregnant person without explicit consent, including shoulder touches, hugs, and proximity adjustments. The medbay corridor is a quiet zone between 2000 and 0600. All requests for visits to the pregnant person must be routed through Dr. Okonkwo. Violations of these protocols will be treated as medical non-compliance and addressed individually.*

She transmitted it to the colony network. Then she sat at her desk and wrote a supplementary note, the one she didn't publish:

*The colony is about to learn the hardest lesson of communal care: that caring for someone sometimes means leaving them alone. I am hopeful they will learn it quickly. I am not confident they will.*

## Scene 3

Jonah fabricated the maternity support brace on his third day of quiet work. It was not in the original medical supply manifest -- Mission AI had listed standard prenatal vitamins, modified mineral supplements, compression stockings, and a set of low-gravity positioning pillows. But Jonah, who had been building things for this colony for seven years, had developed the habit of anticipating needs that no protocol had identified.

He designed the brace from aerospace-grade aluminum and a flexible polymer composite. Lightweight, adjustable, and strong enough to support a growing belly in thirty-eight percent gravity -- a problem Earth engineers had never solved because gravity on Earth was a constant you designed around, not a variable you had to compensate for. In Mars gravity, the belly's effective weight was less, but the distribution of mass changed differently than on Earth, and the woman's center of gravity shifted in ways that terrestrial bracing systems were not designed to accommodate.

Jonah spent twelve hours on the design. He studied the biomechanical models Laila had compiled, cross-referenced them with the low-gravity movement data from the EVA suits, and calculated the optimal support geometry. The brace had three adjustment points -- upper, mid, and lower -- each independently tunable to match the changing body throughout the pregnancy. He added a soft polymer lining where it contacted skin. He added quick-release buckles for emergency removal. He added nothing decorative. It was a tool. It was made by a man who understood that tools, when made correctly, were a form of love.

He delivered it to the medbay on Cycle 1,925. He didn't knock. He left it outside the door with a note:

*Adjustment guide included. Tell Sana to come to fabrication if it needs fitting - I've got the tools and the time. No rush. - J*

He walked away before Laila could find him to say thank you. He had stopped accepting thanks for this kind of work two years ago -- not because the thanks weren't deserved, but because accepting them felt like accepting credit for something that was simply the job.

Arun protected the power margins with the same quiet intensity. He reorganized the colony's electrical distribution map on Cycle 1,920, creating a dedicated circuit for the medbay that was independent of the main habitat bus. The circuit had three redundant feeds: primary from the solar array, secondary from the battery bank, tertiary from the backup generator. If all three failed -- a scenario Arun calculated at 0.03 percent probability -- the medbay's UPS units would sustain critical systems for forty-seven minutes, enough time for Arun to manually restore from the generator.

He ran the power budget on his tablet, staring at the numbers the way he had stared at them during the blackout, during the bioloop crisis, during every moment where the colony's survival had depended on whether the math worked out.

*Current daily consumption: 342 kWh. Solar generation: 380 kWh. Margin: 38 kWh (11.1 percent). Medbay dedicated circuit allocation: 15 kWh/day (includes incubator standby, monitoring equipment, additional climate control). Post-allocation margin: 23 kWh/day (6.7 percent).*

Six point seven percent. Tighter than he preferred. Acceptable. Barely.

He adjusted the colony's power schedule. Non-essential systems would run during peak solar production hours. The robotic fleet's charging cycle would shift to midday when the solar array output peaked. The greenhouse supplemental lighting would dim by ten percent during morning hours -- enough to save four kWh per day, not enough for Mei to lose an argument about it, because Arun had already done the crop yield modeling and ten percent dimming during morning hours had a negligible effect on the tomatoes.

He presented the revised budget to Elena on Cycle 1,922. She reviewed it for six minutes without speaking.

"Six point seven percent," she said.

"It's enough."

"Until something breaks."

"Until something breaks, yes. And if something breaks, we have forty-seven minutes of UPS and the generator."

"And if the generator fails."

"The generator won't fail. I serviced it last week."

"The generator will fail eventually. Everything fails eventually. That's what you taught me."

Arun closed his tablet. "Elena. I am not telling you the margin is generous. I am telling you it's sufficient for the next nine months. After that -- after the birth -- we'll reassess. But right now, the math works. And I don't have a way to make it better without cutting something that someone is relying on."

She nodded. "Keep monitoring. Daily reports. If the margin drops below five percent, I want a colony brief and we start cutting."

"Understood."

"And Arun -- don't lose any sleep over the numbers. You've built the system. The system will hold."

He wanted to believe her. He went back to engineering and ran the numbers again.

Mei adjusted the food priorities on Cycle 1,924. She didn't announce it. She didn't call a meeting. She simply walked into the greenhouse that morning and began rearranging the planting schedule.

The third greenhouse rack had eight growing zones. Zone A: tomatoes, high yield, established crop. Zone B: leafy greens -- kale, spinach, arugula. Zone C: legumes for protein. Zone D: root vegetables -- potatoes, carrots, beets. Zone E: herbs and medicinal plants. Zone F: experimental crops -- quinoa, amaranth, crops being tested for Martian viability. Zone G: the nitrogen-fixing cover crops that enriched the soil. Zone H: currently fallow, resting between cycles.

Mei looked at the zones and began to calculate. The caloric requirements for pregnancy in the first trimester were modest -- an additional hundred calories per day, mostly from protein and complex carbohydrates. By the third trimester, the requirements would reach three hundred additional calories, plus five hundred for lactation. But the quality of the calories mattered more than the quantity. Folate. Iron. Calcium. Omega-3 fatty acids. Nutrients that were difficult to source from a closed-loop agricultural system on a planet with no natural soil.

She increased Zone C's allocation by fifteen percent, shifting space from experimental crops to established legumes. She added a row of spinach to Zone B -- spinach was folate-rich and grew well under LED lighting at Mars atmospheric pressure. She planted a small section of Zone H with amaranth, not as an experiment but as a production crop -- amaranth had a better nutritional profile than the current grain allocation, with more protein per gram and a complete amino acid profile.

She worked for three hours before Tomas found her kneeling in the soil of Zone H, pressing amaranth seeds into the manufactured growing medium with the same tenderness she would use to press a child's hand.

"Mei."

She looked up, soil on her fingers.

"I know what you're doing."

"I'm adjusting priorities."

"I can see that. Zone C is up fifteen percent. Experimental is down. You're planting amaranth in H."

"Yes."

Tomas knelt beside her. He was not good at the emotional parts of colony life -- he was an engineer, a logistics man, a person who tracked inventory and scheduled robot maintenance. But he was good at noticing what people did, even when they didn't say why.

"You're growing food for two," he said.

"For one and a fraction. Now, one and a quarter. It'll increase."

He nodded. "Do you need more robot labor on the harvest cycle."

"I do. The amaranth will need hand pollination. The bees aren't reliable enough at this pressure. I was going to ask you about the small humanoid units -- the ones from the original fleet that do fine motor work."

"I'll reassign them. Three units for hand pollination, scheduled during the light cycle when the plants are most receptive. I can also adjust the greenhouse humidity profile -- if I shift it up three percent, pollination efficiency improves by twelve percent."

Mei looked at him. "You already calculated that."

"I calculated it the day after the vote. Before the pregnancy. Because I knew this day would come. I've been calculating it for two weeks."

She smiled, touched his arm. "Thank you, brother."

"Don't thank me. I'm just doing the job. The same job you're doing. The same job everyone's doing." He paused. "It's different now, though. The job. It's got a reason that's not just survival."

She understood. Survival had been the colony's purpose for seven years. Survive the descent. Survive the first winter. Survive the blackout. Survive the dust storms. Survival was a worthy purpose, but it was a purpose that looked backward, at the threat that had already happened. A pregnancy looked forward, at a thing that would happen. It was a different direction.

Tomas assigned the quiet-duty robots on Cycle 1,928. It was not a glamorous task -- reprogramming movement trajectories, adjusting acoustic dampeners, scheduling maintenance routes that avoided the medbay corridor during designated quiet hours. But he approached it with the same systematic precision he brought to every task.

He identified twelve robots that operated near the medbay on their regular routes. He modified their paths. He adjusted their speed profiles. He reduced the motor torque on their joints to minimize vibration. He installed additional acoustic dampening foam on the units with the loudest cooling fans. He programmed a new behavior: if the robots detected conversation in the corridor, they would pause and wait until the conversation ended before proceeding.

The last change was the most subtle. He adjusted their LED status indicators from white to amber during quiet hours, so that their ambient glow would be warmer, less clinical, more like candlelight than fluorescent. It had zero functional purpose. Amber LEDs consumed the same power as white LEDs. They produced the same amount of light. But the color was different, and different was easier on the eyes when you were lying in a room at 2100 hours, trying to sleep, and a robot was passing by in the corridor.

Tomas tested the changes on Cycle 1,930. He walked the medbay corridor at 2030 hours and recorded the ambient noise level with a decibel meter. Before the modifications: 38 decibels. After: 29 decibels. A nine-decibel reduction -- not dramatic, but perceptible. The difference between hearing a refrigerator hum and hearing nothing at all.

He uploaded the acoustic data to the colony network. No one requested it. No one asked. But Tomas provided it, because data was the only language he fully trusted, and if the numbers said the corridor was quieter, then Laila could trust that the corridor was quieter, and if Laila trusted it, she might sleep.

Gabriel changed his language on Cycle 1,931. It happened without ceremony, without a decision point, without any announcement. He simply stopped using the word "temporary" in his archive entries.

For seven years, the colony had described itself as temporary. The settlement was temporary. The habitat structures were temporary. The power grid was temporary. Everything was temporary, because the original mission plan had called for a three-year stay followed by return to Earth. The return had never happened. The supply chain had collapsed. The colony had remained. But the language had persisted, a linguistic artifact of a plan that no longer existed.

Gabriel's archive entries from Cycle 1 through Cycle 1,930 contained the word "temporary" hundreds of times. *The temporary habitat in Sector B. The temporary greenhouse expansion. The temporary population increase from the latest crew arrival.* Every use of the word carried the implicit promise: we are not staying forever. This is not permanent. This is not home.

On Cycle 1,931, Gabriel sat at the archive terminal and began a new entry. He typed the words that the colony's current situation demanded, and for the first time in seven years of record-keeping, he typed them without hesitation:

*The colony is no longer a temporary outpost. A colony that is hosting its first pregnancy is a colony that has chosen permanence. Whether every colonist voted for this permanence or not, the biological fact of a child being born here -- a child who will have never known Earth, never rained on Earth, never walked under an open Earth sky -- makes the word temporary a fiction. The structures may have been designed with temporary intent. The power grid was built as a temporary solution. The greenhouse was expanded with temporary bracing. But the life that is growing inside a woman in the medbay is not temporary. It is the most permanent thing any of us will ever be part of.*

He saved the entry. Then he went back through the archive and searched for every occurrence of "temporary." There were three hundred and forty-seven. He did not change them. The old entries were the record of what the colony had believed at the time. But he added a footnote to the archive's front page:

*Note: This archive uses language that reflects the colony's evolving understanding of its own permanence. Entries prior to Cycle 1,931 may describe structures, plans, and populations as "temporary." This language reflects the mission plan as it existed at the time of writing, not the colony's current trajectory. The colony chose permanence on Cycle 1,892, when it voted to allow pregnancy. It confirmed that choice on Cycle 1,918, when a body made the decision irreversible.*

Gabriel sat back from the terminal. He looked at the anchor bolts in the ceiling of the archive alcove -- Jonah's anchor bolts, the ones that had held since installation, the ones that would hold for decades if maintained. He thought about the word "permanent" and how strange it felt on his tongue, after seven years of saying "temporary."

Permanent. As if Mars would allow it. As if anything here was guaranteed to persist.

But the child would be born. And whether the colony survived or not, the child would have been born. And that fact -- small, fragile, uncertain, and real -- was a kind of permanence no dust storm or power failure could erase.

## Scene 4

Laila lay awake on Cycle 1,935 at 0247 hours. The medbay was quiet. The amber LEDs of Tomas's modified robots cast a warm glow through the frosted corridor windows. The ventilation fans hummed at their nighttime setting, reduced by ten percent, a sound so constant that Laila noticed it more when it was absent than when it was present.

She lay on the cot in the medbay's private room -- she had stopped going home at night two weeks ago, not officially, not with announcement, just the gradual drift of someone whose presence was more useful in one place than another. Her quarters were eight minutes away. Eight minutes she didn't want to spend walking when she could be in the medbay, monitoring, watching, being close.

0247. She had been awake since 0200.

Her mind was running scenarios. Not medical scenarios -- she knew the medicine. She knew the protocols. She knew the failure modes and the contingency plans and the emergency procedures. What kept her awake were the things that could not be planned, modeled, or rehearsed.

*What if the embryo doesn't implant deeply enough. What if the placenta develops abnormally in low gravity. What if the blood supply doesn't establish properly. What if the heart doesn't form. What if it forms but doesn't beat. What if it beats but beats too fast. What if it beats too slow. What if the neural tube doesn't close. What if the spine doesn't align. What if the bones are too soft. What if they're too hard. What if the lungs don't develop surfactant. What if they do but it's the wrong kind. What if the immune system is compromised because the colony's closed environment hasn't exposed the developing body to the microbial diversity that Earth children receive from soil and air and other people. What if the child is born with no immunity to anything because Mars has no microbes to train it against. What if it's born and the first breath is too violent for the Martian pressure and the lungs tear. What if the first breath is not violent enough and the child doesn't breathe at all. What if the child is born and there is a complication -- umbilical cord prolapse, placental abruption, eclampsia -- and I am too slow or too uncertain or too tired and the outcome is different than it would have been if I had been better.*

She turned over. Pressed her face into the thin pillow. The pillow smelled like recycled fabric and antiseptic and the faint metallic tang of Mars air that never fully filtered out of anything.

She thought about the rat study. Three generations, healthy, mobile, breeding normally. Rats. Not humans. Rats that had been born and had lived and had died in a laboratory cage, and their data was the closest thing to evidence that Mars gravity was compatible with mammalian development. But rats weighed 400 grams. A human infant weighed 3,500. The forces acting on a developing skeleton were orders of magnitude different.

She thought about the incubator. Arun's incubator, tested seven times, with redundant power feeding from three independent sources. The incubator was a good incubator. As good as anything on Earth. But what if the incubator worked perfectly and the baby didn't. What if the incubator was irrelevant because the damage had been done in utero, during development, in the place where no machine could reach.

0322.

She thought about Sana's face three days ago, when the first morning sickness hit. Not dramatic -- a wave of nausea at 0630, a few minutes of sitting very still, a glass of water, and then recovery. Normal. Expected. The body doing what bodies do. But Sana had looked at Laila with such trust, such absolute trust, as if Laila's presence alone could make the nausea stop. And Laila had not been able to make it stop. She had held a basin and waited and offered water and said the things doctors say -- *this is normal, this is expected, this means the hormones are working* -- and none of the words had felt like enough because the words couldn't change the physical reality of Sana's body doing something no human body had ever done on this planet.

0358.

She thought about the four colonists who had voted no. She hadn't asked who they were. She didn't need to know. But she thought about them -- the four people who had looked at the data, at the incubator, at the blood substitute, at the twelve simulation runs, at the twenty-eight percent caloric surplus, at the three people trained in emergency cesarean, at everything the colony had built in five years, and had said no. They were not cruel. They were not afraid. They were honest about the unknowns in a way that the yes-voters had been too hopeful to acknowledge. They had seen the circle of labeled unknowns that Laila had drawn so carefully and had said: *the circle is too big.*

Maybe they were right.

0415.

This was the thought that kept her awake most nights: that the preparation had been sufficient for the known and insufficient for the unknown, and the unknowns were the ones that killed. Medicine was practiced in the gap between what could be predicted and what could not, and every doctor she knew had lost patients in that gap. She had lost patients on Earth -- not many, but enough to know what it felt like to stand over a person you were supposed to save and understand, in the worst possible way, that your knowledge was not enough. The gap had always existed. On Earth, the gap was small, bridged by centuries of data, by the accumulated experience of millions of pregnancies, by the institutional memory of hospitals and medical schools and peer-reviewed journals. On Mars, the gap was the entire distance between the known and the never-been-done.

She sat up at 0430 and walked to the monitoring station. The fetal monitor -- not yet monitoring a fetus, only monitoring Sana's vital signs from her quarters -- displayed steady numbers: heart rate 72, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 14. Normal. Stable. The numbers were a comfort, and the numbers were a lie, because they measured the mother and not the child and the child was the one who could not be measured yet, could not be seen yet, could not be confirmed to exist by anything more than a hormone test and Laila's hope.

She sat at the monitoring station until 0530. Then she went to the mess hall because sleep was no longer possible and food was a biological requirement even when appetite was an emotional impossibility. Gabriel was already there, at his usual corner table, working on the archive. He looked up when she entered.

"Couldn't sleep."

"Couldn't sleep," she confirmed.

He didn't offer advice. He didn't offer comfort. He offered the only thing that Gabriel Winter offered anyone: witness. He closed his notebook and sat with her in silence while she ate cold rehydrated eggs and pretended they were adequate and they weren't, but they were food, and food was a thing the body needed whether it wanted it or not.

After a while, he said: "When I couldn't sleep during the blackout, I used to write. Not archive entries. Personal notes. Things I couldn't put in the official record because they were too uncertain. Too afraid. Too much like the thoughts you're having right now." He reached into his bag and pulled out a folded sheet of paper, old, creased, with yellow edges. "Keep it if you want. Or don't. But know that the thoughts don't make you a bad doctor. They make you a thorough one."

She took the paper. She didn't read it. She put it in her pocket. She would read it later, in the medbay, when the morning shift began and the colony woke and Sana's heart rate appeared on the monitor and the numbers were still normal and the unknowns were still unknown and the work of medicine in a place that had never seen it continued.

## Scene 5

Arun noticed the anomaly on Cycle 1,940. It appeared in the daily electrical inspection log as a minor irregularity -- nothing that would trigger an alarm, nothing that would wake him in the night, nothing that would cause a reasonable person to stop what they were doing and investigate immediately. It was a voltage fluctuation in Habitat Three, Zone D, recorded by a sensor on the secondary subpanel. The fluctuation was small: a 2.3 volt drop over a period of forty seconds, followed by a recovery to nominal levels. The sensor logged it. The system flagged it as a low-priority anomaly. And under normal circumstances, it would have been filed under "monitor" and revisited at the next scheduled inspection.

But the circumstances were not normal. Arun was already operating the colony's power grid at reduced margins. He was already running the medbay on a dedicated circuit with three redundant feeds. He was already recalculating the power budget every morning and finding that the numbers were acceptable but not comfortable. He was already losing sleep over six point seven percent.

So when he saw the 2.3 volt drop in Habitat Three, he didn't file it under "monitor." He filed it under "investigate."

He pulled up the sensor history for Habitat Three, Zone D. The drop had occurred at 1423 hours on Cycle 1,939 -- yesterday -- but he hadn't seen it because yesterday's inspection had been interrupted by the medbay power load test, which had consumed his entire afternoon. He reviewed the twelve-month trend for that specific sensor.

What he found was not dramatic. It was a pattern so gradual that it would have been invisible to anyone not looking for it: over the past eight months, the subpanel in Habitat Three, Zone D had shown an increasing frequency of micro-fluctuations -- not voltage drops, but voltage *noise*. Small oscillations, fractions of a volt, lasting anywhere from two seconds to forty, occurring at irregular intervals. The trend line, if you charted the standard deviation of voltage over time, had a slope. The slope was positive. The noise was increasing.

Arun traced the circuit. Habitat Three, Zone D: this was the secondary living quarters -- six sleeping rooms, a shared lavatory, a small common area. The electrical load in Zone D was modest. Lighting, personal terminal charging, a small environmental control unit. Nothing heavy. Nothing that should be causing voltage noise on a properly functioning circuit.

He ran a diagnostic on the subpanel itself. The results came back clean -- no overheating, no connection resistance above normal thresholds, no signs of moisture intrusion. The subpanel was functioning within its design parameters.

But the voltage noise was real.

He dug deeper. He examined the wiring schematic for Habitat Three -- the original construction drawings from Cycle 15, when the colony had first expanded beyond the ships. The wiring in Habitat Three had not been inspected formally in three years. Not because it was dangerous. Because it was new -- relative to the rest of the colony, which had parts that dated back to the descent -- and because the inspection schedule had been compressed by everything else that had demanded attention: the bioloop, the greenhouse expansion, the medbay buildout, the archive integrity project, the robot fleet maintenance. Three years without a formal electrical inspection wasn't negligence. It was prioritization. And on Mars, prioritization always meant that something got deferred.

He pulled the original installation records. The wiring in Habitat Three had been installed by a team of five people -- not certified electricians, because none of the colonists were certified electricians. They were engineers and fabricators and pilots who had done their best with the materials they had, following electrical schematics transmitted from Earth, using tools that were designed for spacecraft, not buildings. The installation had passed the colony's internal inspection at the time -- a checklist of thirty-two items, all marked "satisfactory."

Arun looked at the checklist. Most of the items were standard: wire gauge verification, connection torque, insulation integrity, grounding continuity. But two items stood out:

*Item 27: Junction box cable strain relief -- satisfactory.*
*Item 28: Wire bundle separation from thermal control lines -- satisfactory.*

Satisfactory. Not optimal. Not inspected by a third party. Satisfactory.

He went to Habitat Three on Cycle 1,941, during the afternoon quiet period when most colonists were on their assigned work shifts. He entered Zone D's electrical closet -- a small room, barely a meter wide, packed with conduit, junction boxes, the subpanel, and the thermal control lines that ran along the ceiling. The closet was not designed for long-term access. It was designed to be sealed and forgotten.

Arun opened the subpanel and began a visual inspection. He had a multimeter in one hand and a flashlight in the other. The flashlight beam swept across the junction boxes, the wire bundles, the connections. At first, he saw nothing unusual. The wiring looked clean. The connections looked tight. The insulation looked intact.

Then he saw the bundle.

It was a cluster of three 14-gauge wires -- the standard gauge for lighting circuits -- that ran from the subpanel to Junction Box 4, which served the Zone D common area. The bundle should have been separated from the thermal control lines by at least five centimeters, per the installation specification. It was separated by less than one. Over the three years since installation, the vibration of the thermal control system -- the expansion and contraction of the pipes as they cycled between heating and cooling -- had caused the wire bundle to rub against the thermal control line. Slowly. Almost imperceptibly. A fraction of a millimeter per cycle. But the cycles added up. Over three years of daily heating and cooling, the cumulative abrasion had worn through the outer insulation on two of the three wires.

The inner insulation was still intact. The wires were not exposed. There was no active short circuit. But the insulation was thin -- paper-thin -- and continuing to thin. When the thermal control lines cycled next -- which they did hundreds of times per day -- the wires would rub again. And again. And eventually, the inner insulation would fail too.

And then there would be a short. And the short would arc. And the arc would generate heat. And the heat would ignite the insulation. And the insulation would burn. And the fire would spread through the wire bundle to the junction box to the subpanel to everything else in the closet.

Arun stood in the electrical closet of Habitat Three, Zone D, with his flashlight illuminating a wire bundle that was slowly wearing itself thin against a thermal control line, and he felt the cold recognition of a danger that had been building for years, incrementally, invisibly, while the colony had been focused on incubators and blood substitutes and prenatal protocols and the most important pregnancy in human history.

He took a photograph with his tablet. He measured the remaining insulation thickness: 0.3 millimeters. The original insulation thickness from the spec sheet: 1.2 millimeters. Seventy-five percent wear.

He closed the subpanel. He exited the closet. He returned to engineering and sat at his desk and stared at the photograph for a very long time.

Then he drafted a report. Not an alarm. Not a panic. A report. Calm, technical, honest.

*ELECTRICAL INSPECTION FINDING -- CYCLE 1,941. Habitat Three, Zone D: Junction Box 4. Wire bundle insulation wear at approximately seventy-five percent of original thickness due to sustained contact with thermal control line. Estimated time to insulation failure: unknown, dependent on thermal cycle frequency, current estimate ranges from thirty to one hundred twenty days before breach. Risk: arc flash, localized fire, potential spread to adjacent circuits. Recommended action: full electrical inspection of Habitat Three, focusing on all wire-to-thermal-line proximity points. Immediate action required for Zone D -- wire rerouting or insulation reinforcement. Full Habitat Three inspection estimated to require forty-eight hours of system downtime.*

He sent the report to Elena. Then he sat in engineering and waited, because waiting was what you did after you identified a danger you couldn't immediately fix, and Arun had spent seven years on Mars learning that dangers identified were not necessarily dangers resolved.

Elena read the report at 1947 hours. She read it twice. She called Arun.

"Forty-eight hours of system downtime," she said.

"Yes."

"Habitat Three houses six people. Plus the common area. If we shut down Habitat Three's power, they lose lighting, environmental control, and terminal access."

"We can run them on backup. The battery bank can support Habitat Three for forty-eight hours. It'll be tight. But they'll have light and heat."

"And the forty-eight hours of downtime means we can't run the medbay power load test we have scheduled for that window."

Arun was quiet. "Yes."

"And the medbay test is part of Laila's prenatal preparedness protocol."

"Yes."

Elena sat with the numbers. The power margin. The pregnancy. The fire risk. The forty-eight hours. She was doing the calculation that no one on Mars wanted to do: weighing a known danger against a scheduled safeguard, choosing between two risks that both had consequences.

"If we delay," she said carefully. "Can we mitigate the immediate risk."

"We can add temporary insulation tape. It'll buy us time. Not much. Maybe a month. But it's not a fix. The only fix is rerouting the wires, which requires --"

"Forty-eight hours of downtime."

"Yes."

"And when can we schedule the forty-eight hours."

"Not during the medbay load test. Not during the harvest cycle in the greenhouse -- Mei says Week 42 is critical for the amaranth. Not during the next solar event monitoring window. I need to find a forty-eight-hour window where the colony can absorb the inconvenience of a partial shutdown and the loss of a scheduled test. It might be three weeks. It might be four."

Elena closed her eyes. "Four weeks is a long time for a wire that's seventy-five percent worn."

"I know."

"And four weeks is a long time when the medbay load test hasn't been run."

"I know."

"Give me tomorrow to think about it. Send the immediate mitigation -- the insulation tape. I want that done today. And Arun --"

"Yes."

"Don't mention this to the colony yet. Not until we have a schedule. I don't want people worried about fires while Sana is in her second month. Let me find the window first."

*Mission AI: Cycle 1,918. Sana's pregnancy test returned positive at 0614 hours. I recorded the result before I reported it to anyone -- a reflex, not a preference. The test detects human chorionic gonadotropin at twenty-five milli-international units per milliliter. ---

## Scene 1

The result appeared on Laila's tablet during breakfast. Not at her desk in the medbay, not in a controlled clinical environment, but at the mess hall table where she was half-listening to Mei discuss nitrogen cycling in the third greenhouse rack while checking her tablet every forty seconds.

Mei was saying something about root-zone pH drift when Laila's tablet vibrated. One short pulse. Result ready.

She looked at the screen.

POSITIVE. 847 mIU/mL. Four to five weeks estimated.

She stared at the number. 847. A number on a screen, derived from a chemical reaction in a plastic stick, representing a cell cluster the size of a poppy seed, dividing in thirty-eight percent gravity on a planet where no human cell had ever divided before outside a Petri dish.

She stood. Her chair scraped the floor. Mei looked up mid-sentence.

"I need to go."

"Did it --?"

"I need to go."

She ran. Past the greenhouse bulkhead, past the connector hall where Jonah's anchor bolts held the ceiling, past the archive terminal. Three minutes and forty-two seconds.

She found Sana in the medbay waiting room, sitting on the bench with Tariq beside her. They had been instructed to wait. They had been waiting for seventeen minutes.

Laila leaned against the doorframe, catching her breath, and delivered the word without any of her professional scaffolding.

"Positive."

Sana made a sound that was not a word. It was the sound the body makes when a reality it has been imagining for five years suddenly becomes a physical fact. Tariq stood. Sat. Stood again. Neither of them spoke for a long time.

Laila composed herself. The professional returned, layer by layer.

"Baseline measurements. Blood work. Ultrasound. We're not declaring victory -- we're declaring presence." She looked at both of them. "And that's everything. For today."

Sana's hand was shaking. She pressed it flat against her thigh, as if she could stabilize herself through bone and fabric alone.

"Four weeks," she said. "We didn't even feel like we'd started."

"The timeline doesn't matter. What matters is that it happened. And now we do the work."

The colony's first pregnancy was beginning within a stable body.

She called Arun first. Not Elena. Arun. Because the incubator was his responsibility, and the power feed to the medbay was his responsibility.

"Arun. It's time."

A pause. Then, quietly: "I'll check the feed."

She called Elena second.

"It happened," Laila said.

"I'm anxious," Laila said.

"So am I."
